summary.text: Evaluating the period identity at \(k=0,1\) gives \(n\mid T^p\) and, after factoring \((T+1)^p-T^p-1=pTU\) with \(U\equiv1\pmod T\), also \(n\mid pT\); conversely these two divisibilities make every non-endpoint binomial term vanish modulo \(n\), since \(p\mid\binom pm\). If \(p^2\mid n\), \(n\mid pT\) forces \(n/p\mid T\), while otherwise cancellation and the primality of \(p\) combine \(n\mid pT\) with \(n\mid T^p\) to force \(n\mid T\); the respective bounds are attained directly.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P_{p,n}(T)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T>0\text{ and }(k+T)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n\text{ for every }k\ge 0.
\]
Thus the period length \(a_p(n)\) is the least positive integer \(T\) satisfying \(P_{p,n}(T)\). We assume throughout that \(p\) is prime and \(n>0\). We shall prove that
\[
a_p(n)=
\begin{cases}
 n/p,&p^2\mid n,\\
 n,&p^2\nmid n.
\end{cases}
\]

The main step is a characterization of the positive periods in terms of two divisibility conditions.

### 1. A binomial auxiliary integer

For every integer \(j\) with \(1\le j<p\), the binomial coefficient \(\binom pj\) is divisible by \(p\). Indeed,
\[
j\binom pj=p\binom{p-1}{j-1}.
\]
Since \(p\) is prime and \(1\le j<p\), we have \(p\nmid j\). Euclid's lemma therefore gives \(p\mid\binom pj\).

For a nonnegative integer \(T\), define
\[
U=U_p(T):=\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\frac{1}{p}\binom pj T^{j-1}.
\]
All the summands are integers by the preceding divisibility. The binomial theorem gives
\[
(T+1)^p=T^p+1+\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\binom pjT^j
          =T^p+1+pTU. \tag{1}
\]
The term corresponding to \(j=1\) in \(U\) is
\[
\frac1p\binom p1T^0=1.
\]
Every remaining term contains a factor \(T\). Hence there is an integer \(V\) such that
\[
U=1+TV. \tag{2}
\]
It follows immediately that
\[
\gcd(T,U)=1, \tag{3}
\]
because any common divisor of \(T\) and \(1+TV\) must divide \(1\). Consequently,
\[
\gcd(T^p,U)=1. \tag{4}
\]

### 2. Necessary divisibility conditions for a period

Suppose that \(T\) is a positive period; that is,
\[
(k+T)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n
\]
for every \(k\ge0\).

Taking \(k=0\), we obtain
\[
T^p\equiv0\pmod n,
\]
so
\[
n\mid T^p. \tag{5}
\]

Taking \(k=1\), we obtain
\[
(T+1)^p\equiv1\pmod n. \tag{6}
\]
Using (1) and (5), congruence (6) becomes
\[
T^p+1+pTU\equiv1\pmod n,
\]
and the term \(T^p\) is already divisible by \(n\). Therefore
\[
n\mid pTU. \tag{7}
\]

By (5), every common divisor of \(n\) and \(U\) is also a common divisor of \(T^p\) and \(U\). In view of (4), this shows that
\[
\gcd(n,U)=1.
\]
We may therefore cancel the factor \(U\) from (7), by Euclid's lemma, and conclude that
\[
n\mid pT. \tag{8}
\]

Thus every positive period \(T\) satisfies both
\[
n\mid T^p\qquad\text{and}\qquad n\mid pT. \tag{9}
\]

### 3. The two divisibilities are also sufficient

Conversely, suppose that \(T>0\) and that
\[
n\mid T^p,\qquad n\mid pT. \tag{10}
\]
We prove that \(T\) is a period.

For any \(k\ge0\), the binomial theorem gives
\[
(k+T)^p
 =\sum_{m=0}^{p}\binom pm k^mT^{p-m}. \tag{11}
\]
The term with \(m=p\) is exactly \(k^p\). The term with \(m=0\) is \(T^p\), which is divisible by \(n\) by (10).

Now consider an intermediate term, where \(0<m<p\). Since \(p\) is prime,
\[
p\mid\binom pm.
\]
Also \(p-m\ge1\), so \(T^{p-m}\) is divisible by \(T\). Hence
\[
\binom pm k^mT^{p-m}
\]
is divisible by \(pT\), and therefore by \(n\), using the second divisibility in (10). Thus every term of (11), apart from the final term \(k^p\), vanishes modulo \(n\). Consequently
\[
(k+T)^p\equiv k^p\pmod n
\]
for every \(k\ge0\).

We have therefore established the useful criterion:

> A positive integer \(T\) is a period of \(k^p\bmod n\) if and only if
> \[
> n\mid T^p\quad\text{and}\quad n\mid pT. \tag{12}
> \]

We now use this criterion to identify the least positive period.

### 4. The case \(p^2\mid n\)

Assume first that \(p^2\mid n\), and put
\[
a=\frac np.
\]
Because \(p\mid n\), this is an integer and
\[
n=pa. \tag{13}
\]
Moreover, \(p^2\mid n\) implies \(p\mid a\). Indeed, writing \(n=p^2r\) gives \(a=pr\).

We first show that \(a\) is a period. From (13),
\[
pa=n,
\]
so certainly \(n\mid pa\). Since \(p\mid a\), we also have
\[
n=pa\mid a^2.
\]
A prime is at least \(2\), so \(p\ge2\), and hence \(a^2\mid a^p\). It follows that
\[
n\mid a^p.
\]
Both conditions in (12) hold, so \(a=n/p\) is a positive period.

It remains to prove minimality. Let \(T\) be any positive period. By the necessary condition (8),
\[
n\mid pT.
\]
Using \(n=pa\), this says
\[
pa\mid pT.
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(p\) yields
\[
a\mid T.
\]
Since \(T>0\), this implies \(T\ge a\). Thus \(a=n/p\) is itself a period and no positive period is smaller. Therefore
\[
a_p(n)=\frac np
\]
when \(p^2\mid n\).

### 5. The case \(p^2\nmid n\)

Now assume that \(p^2\nmid n\). We first show that \(n\) itself is a period. Plainly,
\[
n\mid pn.
\]
Also \(p\ge1\), so \(n\mid n^p\). Hence the criterion (12), with \(T=n\), shows that \(n\) is a positive period.

We prove that every positive period is at least \(n\). Let \(T\) be an arbitrary positive period. Then, by (9),
\[
n\mid pT,\qquad n\mid T^p. \tag{14}
\]
There are two subcases.

#### Subcase 5a: \(p\nmid n\)

Since \(p\) is prime and does not divide \(n\), we have
\[
\gcd(n,p)=1.
\]
From \(n\mid pT\), Euclid's lemma therefore gives
\[
n\mid T.
\]
As \(T>0\), it follows that \(T\ge n\).

#### Subcase 5b: \(p\mid n\)

Write
\[
n=pq,
\qquad q=\frac np. \tag{15}
\]
From \(n\mid pT\), we get
\[
pq\mid pT,
\]
and cancellation of \(p>0\) gives
\[
q\mid T. \tag{16}
\]

Also, since \(p\mid n\) and \(n\mid T^p\), we have
\[
p\mid T^p.
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, a prime dividing a power divides its base. Hence
\[
p\mid T. \tag{17}
\]

We claim that \(p\) and \(q\) are coprime. If \(p\mid q\), then from \(n=pq\) we would get \(p^2\mid n\), contrary to the standing assumption. Since \(p\) is prime and \(p\nmid q\), it follows that
\[
\gcd(p,q)=1. \tag{18}
\]
By (16), (17), and (18), the product \(pq\) divides \(T\). In view of (15), this is exactly
\[
n\mid T.
\]
Again, positivity gives \(T\ge n\).

Thus in every subcase, any positive period \(T\) is at least \(n\). Since \(n\) itself is a period, it is the least positive period. Therefore
\[
a_p(n)=n
\]
when \(p^2\nmid n\).

Combining the two main cases proves
\[
\boxed{
 a_p(n)=
 \begin{cases}
 n/p,&p^2\mid n,\\[2mm]
 n,&p^2\nmid n.
 \end{cases}}
\]
Since in each case the displayed candidate belongs to the nonempty set of positive periods and is no larger than any other member of that set, it is precisely the infimum—and, equivalently for positive integers, the minimum—used in the definition of the period length.
